title: Performance evaluation of a vertical-electrode multi-sampling ionization chamber with Frisch grids for high-rate heavy-ion measurements
abstract: In an ionization chamber, the signal amplitude inherently depends on the position of the ionization track, because the induced signal is determined by the electron drift distance toward the anode. In the stopping layer of a vertical-electrode Multi-Sampling Ionization Chamber (MuSIC), this characteristic leads to an undesired dependence on the ion-stopping depth, which distorts the energy-loss ( Δ E ) correlation and hinders accurate particle identification. To overcome this limitation, Frisch grids were introduced into the stopping layer of the detector. The effectiveness of this configuration was systematically evaluated using an 241 Am α -source and Garfield++ simulations. The experimental results demonstrated that the Frisch grids successfully suppress the dependence of the signal amplitude on the ion-stopping depth. Furthermore, the simulations clarified the geometrical reduction mechanism and examined the optimal grid conditions. Excessively high grid-bias voltages were found to degrade the signal amplitude and energy resolution, likely associated with a reduced electric-field ratio across the Frisch grid, whereas a narrower grid–anode gap more effectively suppressed the distortion in the Δ E correlation.

title: Optimization pathways for a four-tube digital positron lifetime spectrometer
abstract: The count rate and timing resolution are paramount in positron annihilation lifetime spectrometer (PALS), dictating their ability to discern fine-scale material properties. We introduce a compact 4-tube digital PALS (dPALS) configuration that enhances the standard measurement process by capturing 12 spectra simultaneously, reducing measurement times and enabling the observation of rapid material dynamics such as fast kinetics of precipitations in Al-alloys. Our approach allows effective decomposition of 12 spectra, each collected within 2 min with a time resolution of 141 ps and a count rate of 2000 cps. This improved counting rate of the 4-tube PALS system is further complemented by comprehensive tests, aiming at optimizing both digitizer-related and scintillator/photomultiplier tube (PMT) parameters, offering a strategic contribution to improving PALS capabilities for the positron community. Within these tests, we employed, in addition to the 4-tube setup, a 2-tube dPALS, which is still useable by positron researchers. The study's exploration into digitizer parameters such as bandwidth filter, vertical resolution, sampling rate, and constant fraction discriminator (CFD) level indicates that bandwidth alterations do not influence temporal resolution. Utilizing a 10-bit digitizer, we achieved a remarkable enhancement in full width at half maximum (FWHM) by approximately 30 ps compared to an 8-bit system. By setting the sampling rate at 2 GS/s, we attained a minimal FWHM of 124 ps with a 25% CFD level, highlighting a new benchmark for the field. Our comparative assessments have revealed that a fast EJ232Q truncated conical scintillator of 20 cm 3 volume surpasses a cylindrically shaped scintillator of the same material in timing resolution, demonstrating a significant advance in spectrometer design.

The Ring Imaging Cherenkov Detector (RICH) is essential for electron identification within CBM. In this report, an update on the design and construction of the mirror wall is given. title: Fast neutron spectroscopy in CeBr3 via advanced pulse shape discrimination
abstract: Cerium bromide (CeBr 3 ) is an inorganic scintillator offering high scintillation yield, fast decay time, and high energy resolution for γ -ray detection. Unlike similar lanthanide halide materials, CeBr 3 exhibits no particle separation via charge-integral pulse shape discrimination. In this work, we demonstrate the implementation of an advanced waveform-analysis method on scintillation signals from CeBr 3 arising from internal α -particle contamination and 15.2 MeV monoenergetic neutrons. This method successfully separates the γ -ray, proton, and α -particle contributions, achieving a figure of merit up to 1.36. These results show that proton and α signals from fast neutron interactions can be removed from CeBr 3 γ -ray spectra, and that CeBr 3 could have utility for the detection of fast neutrons.

title: Exploring effects of geometrical parameters for CASSIA, a monolithic sensor with internal amplification
abstract: Tracking in future High Energy Physics collider experiments requires high timing and high spatial resolution while keeping the material budget low. The CMOS Active SenSor with Internal Amplification (CASSIA) project addresses these requirements by developing a monolithic CMOS sensor with internal amplification. The sensor is designed to have two operational modes, a low gain amplification region with a gain in the range of 10–100 before breakdown, and a single photon avalanche mode with gain in the order of 1000 after breakdown. In this article, changes to the gain layer radius and implant structures are analyzed, showing a difference in breakdown voltage of tens of volts depending on implant structures and gain layer radius. Dark count rates also show a clear dependence on the combination of n + -electrode and gain layer implants.

title: Development and characterization of a plastic scintillator-based compact test and trigger system with SiPM readout and custom electronics
abstract: We present the design and characterization of a compact, in-house developed plastic scintillator-based trigger system utilizing Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) and custom electronics. The system employs Extruded Plastic Scintillator (EPS) paddles integrated with wavelength-shifting fibers, achieving detection efficiencies exceeding 99%. Using SiPMs instead of traditional PMTs, the design significantly reduces power consumption and physical footprint. The hardware features a custom regulated bias supply and a dedicated front-end electronics chain for signal processing and coincidence logic. Data acquisition is managed by an STM32 microcontroller, providing a cost-effective and flexible alternative to FPGA-based architectures. This modular and user-friendly system offers a scalable solution for high-efficiency cosmic-ray detection and trigger applications.

title: Design and performance of a monolithic plastic scintillator tracker with embedded scatterers
abstract: We propose a new scintillator-based tracker concept based on a monolithic plastic scintillator plate with embedded scatterers and wavelength-shifting fiber readout. The embedded scatterers localize scintillation light so that channels closer to the charged-particle crossing point collect more light. The particle crossing position is reconstructed from the channel-to-channel light yield distribution with a position resolution well below the readout pitch. We performed a positron beam test with prototypes to validate the reconstruction principle and to evaluate the detection efficiency and position resolution. The beam test validated the position reconstruction principle, and demonstrated a near-100% detection efficiency and a position resolution of 1 . 47 mm for normal incidence and 1 . 85 mm for an incidence angle of 45°, with a 10-mm readout pitch. In this paper, we describe the detector concept, the reconstruction method, and the results of the beam test.

title: Design and investigation of a plasma lens for focusing a proton beam at LIGHT
abstract: An active plasma lens (APL) has been designed, constructed, and experimentally commissioned as a collimation device for laser-accelerated proton beams at the LIGHT beamline at GSI. The device consists of a 20 cm long, 4 cm diameter glass capillary filled with low-pressure argon and closed by thin Kapton entrance and exit windows, with coaxial ring electrodes and return conductors enabling a high-current discharge. A dedicated single-stage pulse-forming network based on a 9 µF to 27 µF capacitor bank was built and operated, delivering discharge pulses with peak currents of about 30 kA and microsecond duration, as confirmed by time-resolved current and voltage measurements under laboratory and beamline conditions at LIGHT. The lens has been integrated into the LIGHT beamline and operated during dedicated beam times; analysis of the resulting proton-beam data will be reported separately. A proton-transport simulation is employed as a design tool to define the required discharge-current range and to identify a 7.5 MeV to 8.5 MeV operating window relevant for post-acceleration at LIGHT. The paper focuses on the complete mechanical and electrical realization of a high-current APL for TNSA-driven proton beams and defines its operating parameter space for future detailed beam-transport studies.

title: Design and development of MAPS-based CEPC inner tracker
abstract: The Circular Electron Positron Collider (CEPC) is a next-generation electron-positron collider for precision studies of Higgs, flavor physics and beyond. A key component of its tracking system is the Inner Tracker (ITK) using High Voltage Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor (HV-CMOS) sensor technology. The CEPC ITK consists of three barrel layers and four pairs of endcap disks, covering a total active area of about 20 m 2 . The HV-CMOS sensor fabricated with advanced 55 nm process is used to achieve a few-micrometer spatial resolution and a few-nanosecond timing resolution, with a moderate power consumption. The module design is shared between barrel and endcap to facilitate production. The whole system is designed for minimal material budget, with 0.7% X 0 per layer in the barrel part. The design has been implemented in CEPC software framework for performance study and future optimization.

title: Delayed Phase Neutron Energy (DAPHNE) analysis for discrimination of fissile and fertile uranium
abstract: Active neutron interrogation (ANI) offers a potential approach for verifying nuclear disarmament by detecting special nuclear material in treaty-accountable items. This work introduces the Delayed Phase Neutron Energy (DAPHNE) concept, which exploits the distinct energy spectra of prompt and delayed neutrons to discriminate between highly enriched uranium (HEU) and depleted uranium (DU) in subcritical assemblies. Using a generalized point kinetics model and Monte Carlo N-Particle (MCNP) simulations including realistic detector response, we demonstrate that during the delayed phase following pulsed neutron interrogation, high-multiplication objects containing HEU exhibit a pronounced high-energy neutron component (above 0.5 MeV) that is largely absent in low-multiplication DU objects. This signature arises because delayed neutrons induce secondary fissions in fissile material, producing additional prompt neutrons that are magnified by the high subcritical multiplication factor. Simulations of 25 kg uranium spheres with 14 MeV, 2.5 MeV, and 0.1 MeV neutron sources confirm that the high-energy component remains detectable even through substantial DU shielding, owing to the low absorption cross-sections of fast neutrons. Detector response simulations using a liquid scintillator show that the WGU and DU signatures differ by two to three orders of magnitude in count rate, confirming practical detectability with commercially available equipment. The DAPHNE approach addresses a critical verification challenge by enabling fissile material detection without requiring detailed knowledge of the inspected item’s geometry, which is typically classified information in disarmament contexts.

title: DEMAND: An organic glass scintillator array for direct measurements of (α,n) and (p,n) reactions in inverse kinematics
abstract: We have developed an array of up to 20 organic glass scintillator detectors, each consisting of a $3~\mathrm{cm}\times3~\mathrm{cm}\times3~\mathrm{cm}$ scintillator cube coupled to a photomultiplier tube. Sensitive to neutrons from a few hundred keV to several tens of MeV, the array was designed for use with recoil separators in inverse-kinematics measurements of astrophysical $(\alpha,n)$ and $(p,n)$ reactions. It provides a prompt start signal for identifying recoil-neutron coincidences from the recoil time of flight. We characterize eight detectors used in an inverse-kinematics measurement of $^{22}\mathrm{Ne}(\alpha,n)^{25}\mathrm{Mg}$, using source and in-beam data. From the widths of $\gamma$-ray Compton-edge peaks at 311, 341, 477, and 1062 keVee, we find an energy resolution described by $\mathrm{FWHM}(E)/E=\sqrt{A^2/E+B^2/E^2+C^2}$, with $A=0.00(7)$, $B=0.0618(54)$, and $C=0.135(5)$. The time-difference spectrum of nearest-neighbor $\gamma$-$\gamma$ coincidences from a $^{22}\mathrm{Na}$ source (250--600 keVee) gives a FWHM coincidence timing resolution of $910(40)$ ps, corresponding to a single-detector resolution of $640(30)$ ps. Mixed neutron-$\gamma$ fields from the in-beam reaction and a $^{241}\mathrm{AmBe}$ source show pulse-shape discrimination with an $n$-$\gamma$ figure of merit $>1$ down to about 100 keVee. Below 100 keVee, the total neutron yield can still be extracted using two-Gaussian fits to energy-gated pulse-shape discrimination spectra. Monte Carlo simulations of the present $^{22}\mathrm{Ne}(\alpha,n)^{25}\mathrm{Mg}$ measurement give a neutron singles detection efficiency of $1.56(45)%$, with uncertainty dominated by systematic effects in the simulation inputs.
